# Real-Time Intelligence in Microsoft Fabric: A Complete Practitioner's Guide

## What Is Real-Time Intelligence?

Real-Time Intelligence (RTI) in Microsoft Fabric is a complete, end-to-end solution that covers data ingestion, transformation, storage, modeling, analytics, visualization, and automated actions — purpose-built for event-driven and streaming scenarios [S1]. Unlike bolt-on streaming add-ons that require stitching together separate products, RTI is a native, first-class workload inside Fabric, sharing the same capacity, governance, and OneLake foundation as every other Fabric experience.

If you have worked with platforms where streaming and batch analytics lived in entirely separate stacks, RTI changes that equation. A single Fabric capacity budget covers your real-time pipelines, your analytical store, your alerting engine, and your visualization layer — and every component can read from or write to the same OneLake storage without data copies.

## The Architecture at a Glance

![Real-Time Intelligence flow](/content/diagrams/rti-flow.svg)

The RTI workload assembles five major building blocks:

1. **Real-Time hub** — a tenant-wide catalog of data in motion
2. **Eventstreams** — no-code streaming pipelines
3. **Eventhouse / KQL databases** — the analytical store for time-series and streaming data
4. **Activator** — the automated-action engine
5. **Map** — built-in geospatial visualization

These components are not independent products requiring separate deployments; they are experiences within a single Fabric workspace item namespace, integrated through shared events and the Real-Time hub.

---

## Core Concepts

### Real-Time Hub: The Tenant-Wide Catalog of Data in Motion

The Real-Time hub is the tenant-wide counterpart of OneLake for data in motion: it catalogs eventstreams, KQL database tables, Microsoft-managed source streams, and Fabric/Azure events so users across the organization can discover, ingest, and react to streaming data from one place [S2].

More specifically, Real-Time hub surfaces active data streams alongside Microsoft-managed sources — including CDC feeds from Azure SQL Database, Azure Cosmos DB, and Azure Database for PostgreSQL — and Fabric workspace item events, making all of these accessible to every Fabric workload [S1]. This means a data scientist, a warehouse engineer, and an operations analyst can all discover the same live data streams without coordinating through a central team; discovery is self-service and governed through standard Fabric permissions.

The design deliberately mirrors how OneLake made batch data discoverable across workloads. *Inference:* just as OneLake eliminated the need for separate data lake accounts per team, Real-Time hub aims to eliminate the proliferation of disconnected Kafka topics, event grids, and CDC pipelines that different groups manage in isolation.

### Eventstreams: No-Code Streaming Pipelines

Eventstreams provide a no-code pipeline for collecting, transforming, and routing high-volume real-time data to multiple destinations simultaneously [S1]. This is the ingestion and routing layer of RTI.

On the source side, supported connectors include Apache Kafka, AWS Kinesis, Google Cloud Pub/Sub, MQTT v3.1/v3.1.1, and a dedicated MQTT-based Real-Time Weather connector [S1]. This breadth of protocol support means RTI is not locked to Azure-native event sources: IoT devices, cross-cloud Kafka clusters, and third-party SaaS event streams can all feed the same Eventstream.

Eventstreams also expose built-in stream processing operators — filtering, cleansing, windowed aggregations, deduplication, and content-based routing — so data can be shaped before it lands at a destination [S1]. You do not need a separate Spark Structured Streaming job or Azure Stream Analytics resource for common transformation patterns; the Eventstream designer handles them inline.

Transformations inside an Eventstream can produce **derived eventstreams**: reusable, shareable outputs that downstream consumers can subscribe to independently [S1]. This lets a single raw IoT feed be transformed into multiple purpose-fit streams — one filtered to high-severity events for alerting, another aggregated to per-minute summaries for dashboards — without duplicating the source connection.

### Eventhouse and KQL Databases: The Analytical Store

While not represented by a verified claim in the current knowledge base beyond what appears in the claims above, Eventhouse is the storage and query layer for RTI, exposed through KQL (Kusto Query Language) databases. The eventhouse source registered in this knowledge base (tier 1, Microsoft Learn) confirms Eventhouse is a first-class RTI item, tagged with KQL, KQLDatabase, and OneLake integration. *Inference:* Eventhouse stores streaming data in a columnar, time-indexed format optimized for append-heavy, time-series workloads, and integrates with OneLake so that data is accessible to non-RTI Fabric workloads without a copy.

Fabric notebooks can operate directly over Eventhouse data using KQL, T-SQL, Python, or Spark without requiring data movement, unifying exploration, transformation, and machine learning within a single authoring surface [S1]. This is a significant practitioner benefit: you can write a KQL query to inspect live data, then switch to Python in the same notebook to train an anomaly detection model on the same Eventhouse dataset, with no ETL step between them.

### Activator: Threshold, Pattern, and KQL-Defined Automated Actions

Activator monitors data flowing through Real-Time hub, KQL queries, or Power BI reports and fires automated actions when conditions are met [S1]. The supported condition types are:

- **Threshold conditions** — a value crossing an upper or lower bound
- **Pattern conditions** — sequences or absence of expected events
- **KQL-defined conditions** — arbitrary logic expressed as a KQL query

When a condition fires, Activator can take one or more of the following actions [S1]:
- Send notifications (email, Teams)
- Launch a Fabric pipeline execution
- Trigger a Spark job
- Run a Dataflow
- Call a User Data Function (serverless function within Fabric)
- Trigger a Power Automate workflow

This range of action types means Activator is not simply a notification service. It is an orchestration engine that can kick off complex multi-step batch or streaming processes in response to real-time signals.

Fabric events and Azure Blob Storage events exposed in Real-Time hub can trigger Activator rules to start Spark jobs or Dataflows, enabling fully event-driven orchestration that requires no polling schedule [S1]. This eliminates the classic antipattern of a scheduled pipeline running every five minutes to check whether something changed — the pipeline only runs when the event actually occurs.

### AI and Conversational Analytics Integration

RTI integrates with Fabric data agents to enable conversational analytics and workflow orchestration over Eventhouse data, complementing Activator's threshold-based alert automation with reasoning over live and historical datasets [S1]. *Inference:* this positions RTI not just as a real-time dashboard layer but as an AI-accessible operational data store, where a copilot or agent can answer natural-language questions about current event streams and trigger downstream actions.

### Geospatial Analytics with Map

Real-Time Intelligence supports geospatial analytics through Map, a built-in visualization experience that layers bubbles, heatmaps, polygons, and 3D extrusions over Eventhouse or Lakehouse data [S1]. Map supports configurable KQL refresh intervals, so the map updates live as new events arrive — making it suitable for tracking fleets, monitoring sensor networks, or visualizing geographic event distributions in real time [S1].

---

## How RTI Fits Into the Broader Fabric Platform

### Integration with Data Factory Pipelines

Pipeline storage-event triggers in Data Factory consume RTI components: the event flow runs through an Eventstream and the trigger rule lives in Activator, so trigger management happens partly in those RTI experiences rather than only in the pipeline editor [S3]. This is an important operational detail: if you are building event-triggered pipelines and wonder why the trigger configuration takes you outside the pipeline canvas, that is by design — the event routing and condition evaluation live in RTI.

This means teams responsible for pipeline operations need at minimum a working knowledge of Activator and Real-Time hub, even if they do not otherwise work with streaming data.

### Event-Driven Orchestration Without Polling

Fabric events and Azure Blob Storage events exposed in Real-Time hub can trigger Activator rules to start Spark jobs or Dataflows, enabling fully event-driven orchestration [S1]. *Inference:* in a well-designed RTI-integrated architecture, the scheduled trigger becomes the exception rather than the rule. Most orchestration reacts to actual data arrival or state changes, improving both latency and resource efficiency.

---

## Best Practices

The following practices emerge from the verified architecture claims above:

**Use derived eventstreams for multi-consumer scenarios.** When a single source feeds multiple downstream use cases (alerting, dashboards, archival), produce derived eventstreams from the primary Eventstream rather than creating multiple source connections [S1]. This reduces connection overhead and ensures all consumers see the same transformation logic.

**Apply Eventstream operators before landing data.** Filtering, deduplication, and windowed aggregations inside the Eventstream reduce the volume of data written to Eventhouse or other destinations [S1]. Cleaning data in-flight is far cheaper than storing raw events and cleaning them at query time.

**Use KQL-defined Activator conditions for complex logic.** Simple threshold conditions are easy to define but cannot express composite or stateful logic. Where you need to detect patterns across multiple fields or time windows, prefer KQL-defined conditions in Activator [S1].

**Leverage Real-Time hub for cross-team stream discovery before creating new sources.** Before building a new Eventstream connection, check Real-Time hub for existing streams covering the same data [S2, S1]. Reusing an existing stream avoids duplicate ingestion costs and keeps the catalog coherent.

**Use event-driven Activator triggers rather than scheduled pipelines where possible.** Fabric events in Real-Time hub can trigger Spark jobs and Dataflows without a polling schedule [S1]. Prefer this pattern for latency-sensitive workloads; reserve scheduled triggers for cases where a fixed cadence is genuinely required.

**Operate over Eventhouse data from notebooks without data movement.** Fabric notebooks support KQL, T-SQL, Python, and Spark against Eventhouse directly [S1]. There is no need to export Eventhouse data to a Lakehouse to run exploratory analysis or train a model; use the notebook's multi-language support to work with the data in place.

---

## What Goes Wrong

No antipattern-type claims are currently verified in the knowledge base for this capability. The following are *Inference:* warnings based on the architecture claims above and general streaming platform experience — not verified facts.

*Inference:* **Ignoring the Activator/Eventstream split in pipeline trigger management.** Teams that expect pipeline event triggers to be configured entirely within the pipeline editor will be confused when they are redirected to Activator and Eventstream. Understanding that trigger state lives in RTI is essential for troubleshooting and access control [S3].

*Inference:* **Treating Real-Time hub as a fire-and-forget inbox.** Because Real-Time hub surfaces CDC feeds from Azure SQL DB, Cosmos DB, and PostgreSQL, it is tempting to subscribe to every available feed. Without governance on which streams are consumed and by whom, the hub can become a sprawling catalog that is hard to audit.

*Inference:* **Skipping stream transformation and writing raw events to Eventhouse.** Eventhouse stores are optimized for query performance over well-shaped data. Ingesting highly variable, un-filtered raw events and expecting to clean them at query time increases both storage costs and query complexity.

## Worked Example: Event-Driven Fleet Monitoring

The following scenario illustrates how the verified RTI architecture operates end-to-end. Steps labelled *Inference:* go beyond the verified claims.

**Scenario:** A logistics company tracks 5,000 delivery vehicles via MQTT telemetry. They need live map visibility, automated alerts when a vehicle stops unexpectedly, and a daily Spark job to retrain their route-optimization model.

1. **Ingestion.** An Eventstream is created with an MQTT v3.1.1 source connector pointed at the vehicle telemetry broker [S1]. The Eventstream runs a deduplication operator (in case the same GPS ping is sent twice) and a content-based routing operator that splits high-severity events (engine-off, geofence breach) from normal location updates [S1].

2. **Derived streams.** Two derived eventstreams are produced: one for all location pings routed to Eventhouse for storage and map rendering, and one for high-severity events routed to Activator [S1].

3. **Live map.** The Map experience in RTI connects to the Eventhouse location table with a KQL refresh interval of 10 seconds, rendering vehicle positions as bubbles and geofence polygons as polygon overlays [S1].

4. **Alerting.** Activator monitors the high-severity derived eventstream with a KQL-defined condition that fires when a vehicle has had no location update for more than 3 minutes during working hours [S1]. On firing, Activator sends a Teams notification and launches a Fabric pipeline to open an incident ticket via Power Automate [S1].

5. **Model retraining.** A Fabric workspace event — "pipeline run completed" for the nightly data preparation pipeline — is exposed in Real-Time hub [S1]. An Activator rule monitors this event and triggers the Spark training job directly, eliminating the need for a scheduled trigger on the Spark job itself [S1].

6. **Exploration.** A data scientist opens a Fabric notebook, writes a KQL query against the Eventhouse location table to identify routes with the most stop events, then switches to Python in the same notebook to build a clustering model — no data export required [S1].

*Inference:* The entire stack above runs within a single Fabric capacity. The Map, Activator rules, Eventstream connectors, and Eventhouse KQL database all live in the same workspace and are visible to the same set of workspace members.
